stops.name: Marbach am Neckar, the tailor's house, Niklastorstraße
stops.campa: On a wet November day, in a single rented room on the ground floor of the tailor Schöllkopf's house, Elisabetha Dorothea bears her only son. The regimental surgeon and recruiting-officer Johann Caspar Schiller is away with the Duke's soldiers; his wife has come here with two-year-old Christophine. They name him Johann Christoph Friedrich. The house is narrow, the fortunes narrow; the child spends only his first four years within these walls beside the Neckar. Out of this cramped Württemberg beginning will come the poet of freedom.

stops.name: Lorch, the pastor's boy, the first Latin
stops.campa: The father is posted to Lorch, and here in the shadow of the old Hohenstaufen monastery the boy's schooling begins. Pastor Philipp Moser teaches him his first Latin and his catechism, and the child conceives an early wish to enter the Church and preach. He plays at holding sermons, draping a black pinafore for a cassock. The piety of these Swabian years, the hymnbook, the pulpit imagined, never wholly leaves the man who will write the Ode to Joy.

stops.name: Ludwigsburg, the Latin school, the ducal garrison
stops.campa: The family removes to Ludwigsburg, the Duke's baroque garrison-city, and from January 1767 Friedrich attends the Latin school. Here he first sees theatre, the court's opera and its French comedians, and the splendor of Karl Eugen's court dazzles the boy. He is confirmed, still meaning for the ministry. But the Duke, who founds his soldiers' orphanage into a military academy, has marked the promising sons of his officers. A summons is coming that no officer's family may refuse.

stops.name: Schloss Solitude, enrolled the 447th pupil
stops.campa: On 16 January his father leads him through the gates of the Duke's academy at the hunting-palace Solitude, above Stuttgart. He is thirteen, entered as the 447th pupil into the Hohe Karlsschule, that same year raised to the rank of a military academy. The wish for the pulpit is denied him: theology is not taught here. He is set to the law, which he loathes. The discipline is total: every hour drilled, letters censored, the Duke a father-god watching all. The boy of freedom is caged.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Karlsschule, medicine and Die Räuber by candle
stops.campa: The academy is moved down into Stuttgart, and Schiller abandons law for medicine. But behind the medical drill another work grows: by stolen candlelight, hidden from the masters, he writes Die Räuber, the tale of the noble outlaw Karl Moor who declares war on a corrupt world. The forbidden Sturm und Drang burns in him; he reads Shakespeare and Rousseau in secret. In 1780 he graduates doctor of medicine and is made a regimental surgeon on wretched pay, forced to wear the Duke's uniform.
stops.quote_source: Motto placed on the second edition of Die Räuber (1782), with a rampant lion

stops.name: Mannheim, the premiere at the Nationaltheater
stops.campa: Without his sovereign's leave, the young surgeon slips across the border to Mannheim to see his robbers live upon the stage. On 13 January the Nationaltheater plays Die Räuber, Iffland as Franz Moor, and the house becomes a madhouse: rolling eyes, clenched fists, hoarse cries, strangers falling into one another's arms, women staggering faint to the doors. In a single night the twenty-two-year-old regimental doctor is famous through Germany. He has tasted the world beyond the Duke's wall, and cannot go back to the cage.
stops.quote: The theatre resembled a madhouse — rolling eyes, clenched fists, hoarse outcries in the audience. Strangers fell sobbing into each other's arms, women staggered to the door close to fainting. It was a general dissolution, as of chaos, out of whose mists a new creation bursts forth.
stops.quote_source: Contemporary account of the Mannheim premiere, 13 January 1782

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Duke's arrest and the ban on poetry
stops.campa: For the unlicensed journey to Mannheim the Duke has him arrested a fortnight, and issues the order that seals Schiller's fate: he is forbidden, on pain of prison, to write anything but medicine: no more plays, no more 'comedies,' no correspondence beyond Württemberg. To the poet this is death. He resolves to desert. He waits his chance while the Duke prepares a great festival with fireworks for the visiting Russian Grand Duke Paul.
stops.quote: Der Herzog will nicht, dass ich schreibe. Also muss ich fort.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Schiller in the biographical tradition of the flight

stops.name: The night flight from Stuttgart, with Andreas Streicher
stops.campa: On the night of 22–23 September, while the Duke's fireworks burst over the city for the Russian prince, Schiller and his loyal friend the musician Andreas Streicher pass unseen through the gate. The deserter-poet is out of Württemberg forever. He carries the manuscripts of Fiesko and of a bourgeois tragedy, Luise Millerin. Behind him lie his oath as an officer, his family, his native land; before him, poverty, hiding, and the whole of German literature.

stops.name: Oggersheim, the fugitive under the name Dr. Ritter
stops.campa: The two fugitives lodge at the Viehhof inn in Oggersheim near the Rhine, and here, hunted and near penniless, Schiller takes the false name Dr. Ritter. He finishes Fiesko and drives forward Luise Millerin. But Mannheim's theatre-manager Dalberg dares not employ a deserter the Duke may reclaim; the work will not be staged, the purse is empty. A rescuer appears: Henriette von Wolzogen, mother of his schoolfellow, offers him refuge on her Thuringian estate.

stops.name: Bauerbach, asylum with Henriette von Wolzogen
stops.campa: In December Schiller reaches the quiet estate of Bauerbach near Meiningen, given asylum by Henriette von Wolzogen. Under the name Dr. Ritter he lives here more than half a year, sheltered and fed, and out of this peace comes Kabale und Liebe, the bourgeois tragedy of Louise Miller and Ferdinand, an indictment of princely tyranny that his own Duke had all but authored. He drafts, too, the first outline of Don Karlos, the drama of freedom of thought. A poor librarian's daughter stirs his heart.
stops.quote_source: Marquis Posa to King Philip, Don Karlos (III.10), conceived in these years

stops.name: Mannheim, theatre-poet, fever, and the road out
stops.campa: Dalberg at last engages him as house-poet of the Nationaltheater. In one year Fiesko and Kabale und Liebe are given; the latter triumphs. But a malignant fever nearly kills him, debts pile, the contract is not renewed, and a hopeless love for the married Charlotte von Kalb torments him. Sick, poor, and restless, Schiller looks eastward, where an admirer, a stranger named Körner, has written to him out of Leipzig with words of pure devotion.

stops.name: Leipzig, met by the friends who summoned him
stops.campa: Schiller comes to Leipzig, the city of his dreams, where the young Körner and his circle, the Stock sisters, the publisher Göschen, Ludwig Ferdinand Huber, have called this admired stranger to them out of love alone. They lift his debts, they take him in. 'Leipzig appears to my dreams,' he writes, 'like the rosy morning beyond the wooded hills.' Here, among true friends, the bitter years break and joy returns to him, and demands a song.
stops.quote: Leipzig erscheint meinen Träumen und Ahndungen wie der rosigte Morgen jenseits den waldigen Hügeln. In meinem Leben erinnere ich mich keiner so innigen prophetischen Gewissheit, wie diese ist, dass ich in Leipzig glücklich seyn werde.
